en: RAS no. 52 (ff. 13, paper, common Newārī script): *Tantraślokasaṃgraha* by Jīvaharṣa [1v] [Siddham] Homage to the Buddha!
I bow down to the Guru-Buddha, the Guru-Dharma, and likewise the Guru-Saṅgha; I bow down to the Guru-Vajradhara and to the Guru who is everything. (1)
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara; the Guru is the omnipresent perfection, the Guru is the teacher of the three worlds. || 2 ||
Obeisance be to you, O Sarvasiddha; obeisance again and again to you, O Sarvadevī.
Obeisance be to you, O Sarvadaitya; likewise [obeisance] to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. (3)
As long as old age does not prevail— since disease is indeed difficult to ward off, nor grief, nor separation from a beloved, nor the misfortune that binds one to affection—
[one should realize] that which is called Śiva: the form of space, free from mind, with its drops diminished.
For that long, let the wise contemplate that liberation, which is supreme bliss. || 4 ||
First the body, then the wind, and likewise the mind as the third;
such is the means for accomplishing the siddhi of the omniscient Buddha who possesses all qualities. (5)
The syllable is to be accomplished through the body; it is the immovable state through the multitude [of atoms].
It is mindless, yet from the continuum of the mind, through the singular yoga of the vajra-ground. (6)
From the breath comes longevity; from the drop comes the body; from the perfectly unmoving mind comes liberation.
When these three have become motionless, that triad is exceedingly difficult to attain.
Thus is what was stated in the four verses of the Vajrakavaca.
The deity does not exist in wood, nor does he exist in stone;
for the deity exists in the mental state (bhāva). Therefore, the mental state is most excellent.
Deities do not exist within substances, in wood, in clay, in stone, or in paintings;
for all deities are but transformations of the mind.
Therefore, O God, the mind alone is indeed the certain [means]. || 9 ||
There is nothing higher than the self as god; for the self as god is indeed supreme. For those who are attached to the self as god, it is like [the futility of] worshipping an image. || 10 ||
Through the consecration of mantras, even wood and such attain the state of a deity;
how much more so the body of one possessing knowledge, which is yet as motionless as a log of wood? (11)
Even a Buddha made of stone or wood grants liberation within a hundred thousand lifetimes;
how much more so that which is eternal, even in this very life?
The guru bestows liberation with reverence. || 12 ||
Beholding the virtuous is meritorious, for the virtuous are indeed like sacred pilgrimage sites and deities;
a pilgrimage site yields fruit in time, but the company of the virtuous yields fruit immediately.
The opportune moment (kṣaṇa), free from the eight inopportune states, is extremely difficult to obtain;
it is comparable to a turtle placing its neck through the hole of a yoke floating upon the great ocean. 14.
Hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, barbarians, long-lived gods,
those with wrong views, the two [extremes of] Buddhahood and solitary enlightenment, and muteness— these are the eight unfavorable conditions here.
This has been stated in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra* [at 1.4]: || 15 ||
One should abandon laziness, sleep, desire, and the censuring of anger, delusion, and the like;
and one should cast off hunger, bodily pain, and Māra by means of terrifying [meditations]. 16.
All faults are overcome: 1. laziness by diligence; 2. sleep by wholesome activity; 3. falling into existence by anger; 4. the loss of mindfulness by those possessed by desire;
5. the delusion of one who reviles the deluded; 6. the turning wheel of existence by craving.
And for one who lacks respect due to hunger, he should abandon Māra seven times. || 17 ||
"The seven Māras."
Having obtained a human birth so difficult to attain,
he who does not set his mind upon the paths to liberation is a beast on this earth, merely lacking horns.
He remains in human form, with his weapons cast aside.
This has been stated in the Mohamudgara: || 18 ||
For the speakers of Dharma are themselves Dharma, and the listeners are likewise so;
the cessation of intrinsic natures is Dharma, which is none other than emptiness itself.
This has been stated in the *Nāmasaṃgītiṭīkā* [at folio] 6r–6v. || 19 ||
As long as the mind does not dissolve into the non-conceptual Self, what is the use of postures, meditative absorptions, recitations, and yogic practices?
Just as a broken jar cannot hold water, [so too the mind that has not dissolved cannot sustain the state].
The jar is not established as long as it has not yet come into contact with its cause.
The thought of awakening (bodhicitta) must always be protected, for it is the cause of the cessation of suffering;
otherwise, there will be no accomplishment even in tens of millions of incalculable eons.
The Lord of the World, the thought of awakening, shines forth through the manifestation of all things;
he illuminates every limb as the very self of the Lord of the World throughout the entire universe.
The Bindu is the Buddha, the Bindu is Śiva, the Bindu is Viṣṇu, and the Bindu is Prajāpati;
the Bindu is the all-pervading God, the Bindu is the mirror of the three worlds.
It is stated in the *Amṛtasiddhi* (7.15) regarding the *Amṛtasiddhi-yoga*: [23]
Sensual desire, when pursued by the ignorant, becomes a bond;
yet that very same desire, when pursued by the wise, is the means for achieving liberation. (24)

When the drop (bindu) enters the midst of the womb, the merit of ten million offerings perishes; there is the loss of sacred pilgrimage sites and the loss of ascetic merit, and at every step one incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin. (Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa 42, verse 25)
Not knowing Mahāmudrā and relying solely on the practice of Karmamudrā, those practitioners fall away from the reality of the oral tradition and go to the Raurava hell. (26)
Sekanirdeśa 39:
With the vajra, the wheel [is turned] in the six realms for the destruction of evil deeds;
for that vajra is indeed the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), which eradicates all afflictions. || 27 ||
The drop (bindu) that flows from the forehead is called Viṣṇu because of its entry;
even though it is endowed with the Vedas, in the Hevajra [tantra] it is Śiva for seven kalpas. (28)
The appearance—excellent and lovely—is merely dependent origination;
if it did not exist, emptiness would be considered a dead woman indeed.
The fivefold [treatise on] passion has been explained in the *Prajñopāyapañcaka* (29).
When the dharmadhātu is neither self, nor female, male, or neuter,
and is completely liberated from all grasping, how can it be conceptualized as a "self"?
Thus it was said by the venerable Nāgārjuna. || 30 ||
One who holds the firm vajra should meditate upon everything as consisting of the mind-vajra;
for this is declared to be the commitment (samaya) of those who realize the indivisibility of the three vajras.
That has been stated in the *Guhyasamāja* [17.28]. //31//
Because reality is awakened as true bliss through the awakening of delight,
and because this occurs within the body, it is therefore called "deity" (devatā).
It is stated in the *Hevajratantra*, chapter I, verse 14: [32]
The Blessed One takes the form of semen, and that bliss is known as the beloved;
it is not for Pratyekabuddhas, nor is it within the range of Śrāvakas. (Hevajra I.viii.50ab)
It is also quoted in the *Jñāneśvarīmāhātmya* on page 58: "And it is said in the *Khasama Tantra*: 'It is within the range of the *śrāvakas*. (33)
The *patta* is declared to be the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), and the deity is the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
The knower of yoga should always worship her in the form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
It is stated in the *Hevajrapañjara*: || 34 ||

Furthermore, this other [state], which has the nature of waking and dreaming, and the nature of deep sleep and the fourth (turya), moves through sense objects while residing in the body, merged with the breath,
yet unmoving when merged in the mind; it resides in gnosis, and even for a moment during sexual union, it becomes the awakened mind when [the vital energy] is melted.
The mind-vajra certainly arises in four ways from emanation and so forth in succession. (35)

Thus, the mind—which exists in four ways within the threefold existence of living beings—is to be protected by the lords of yogins within the center of the *bindu*, for the sake of liberation; it is all-pervasive and bestows the fruit of equal bliss. (Kālacakra 5.125)

If even a drop [of semen] is released, where is liberation for yogis who have attained supreme bliss? Since it is the seed of rebirth, this momentary pleasure of worldly existence must always be avoided by ascetics here.
That has been stated in the *Kālacakra*: [verse 5.126]. 36.
A small amount of warm Akṣobhya water pacifies mouth ailments and toothache;
Akṣobhya used as a nasal drop at dawn removes headaches. Likewise, urine—whether warm or cold—when introduced into the ears or eyes, removes pain from both.
When bitten by a venomous creature, [the application of] Akṣobhya-nasya combined with the three pungents (trikaṭuka) bestows well-being.
It is stated in the *Kālacakra* (2.124): [37]

One who causes suffering to living beings, who is harsh toward his teacher, who holds false views, who is cruel and merciless, and who is motivated by envy, deceit, greed, and wealth—what state of woe would not result from such wickedness? (38)
An impure mind is the teacher’s mouth;
even when fevers have increased, the drinking of ghee given [therein] brings about great immortality for the auspicious.
Through delusion, one's own mind is obstructed by the Buddhas. || 39 ||
As long as you perform worship of your own body, which by its very nature wanders through the difficult wilderness of saṃsāra,
why indeed do you not perform that same worship of the Guru?
She who bestows the entirety of the bliss of nirvāṇa. || 40 ||
In the *Paramārthasevā*,
verse 66: It is indeed with priceless jewels that deer and birds are lured, while for the donkey, it is merely desirable fodder.
A lamp for the blind, music for the deaf—what is the Dharma for a fool? Where is the occasion for it?
It is stated in the Sārasaṃketaka: || 41 ||
He who does not create division even among beings who are already divided becomes one with a steadfast mind and an inseparable retinue. (42)
The sixfold constituents of all sentient beings are non-different and consist of the five elements;
yet, by making them appear divided, a sentient being is born into a lowly family.
It is stated in the *Ṣaḍgatikā*: || 43 ||
Those phonemes which have been described as being at the back, and those which are again facing forward,
as well as those categorized as feminine, masculine, and neuter, and those conceived as the elements and so forth—
It is stated in the *Hevajrapañjara* [in the *Pañcakrama*, verse 1.38]: || 44 ||
The eye is the Buddha Vairocana; the ear is Vajrasūryaka;
the nose is Paramāśva; and the mouth is Padmanarteśvara.
The body is King Śrī Heruka, and the mind is Vajrasattva;
thus, the yogin, whose nature is compassion, should always conduct himself correctly. (45)
In the *Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa*, verses 77–78:
Brahmā resides in the center of the navel, while Mādhava resides in the center of the heart;
Śaṅkara is to be known as being in the head. These three locations bestow liberation.
Gorakṣayogaśāstra 34: The wise, through austerities, emaciate their bodies,
knowing that the mind is the cause of the body's transformations.
Out of anger, he destroys the one who has hurled a weapon at hundreds of others, even before that weapon has been released.
This has been stated regarding the purification of the mind. || 47 ||
Aquatic creatures are born and die even in the water;
yet human beings do not go to heaven merely by bathing.
It is stated in the Itihāsa-śāstra: || 48 ||
Lust, hatred, delusion, envy, thirst, and so forth are always declared to be the root of all evils; this [root] is not purified by bathing.
In the *Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa*, it is stated regarding the purification of the mind: || 49 ||
For those who are esteemed by the wise—truth, generosity, and patience—and especially compassion, what need have they for extensive discourses on dharma? (50)
By taking this impure image and making it an image of the jewel-like Victor, one makes it priceless.
Take up with great firmness that which is born of flavor, exceedingly piercing, and known as the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
It is said in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*: [1.10] || 51 ||
The seed of suffering sown in the mind increases even over the course of many lifetimes;
therefore, it should be avoided by those who are pure.
Having reflected, equal happiness is desired. || 52 ||
The innate (*sahaja*) nature of all phenomena consists of the essence of one's own bliss;
it is self-established (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) due to its self-arisen state, and unstruck (*anāhata*) because it is indestructible. (53)
Samvarodaya 3.13cd–14ab and Sthitisamāsa 164: That which is free from the conventional discourse of existence and non-existence is neither of the nature of merit nor of the nature of sin.
The Buddhas proclaim that which is the foremost state, consisting of neither merit nor sin, to be entirely empty.

The afflictions are not distinct from awakening, nor do afflictions arise within awakening. The conceptualization of afflictions arises from delusion; delusion itself is by nature immaculate. (Pañcakrama 4.21)
Mahāyānaviṃśikā 8; also Yogāmbaramahātantra 1.35:
In order to lead them into the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*), their distinction [from others] has been demonstrated.
Through the instruction of a true guru, this becomes clear, and not otherwise.
It is stated in the *Samvarodayatantra* (3.16cd–17ab) and also in the *Sthitisamāsa* (170cd–171ab): [56]
In the beginning, the Blessed Lady Prajñā should not be served by people of weak faculties;
otherwise, there will be no accomplishment at all until the *rasa* is mastered. (57)
Fire never possesses the nature of an enemy toward mercury; a goldsmith is never devoid of fire;
a maker of gold is never unbound; and for those who speak, enjoyments are never devoid of gold. Likewise, the binding of the mind for yogis is never truly devoid of union with the Consort.
One who is not bound does not pierce the body; here, one whose body is unpierced bestows innate bliss.
Kālacakra 4.224:
If a lump of iron, when thrown into water, sinks by itself alone;
yet that very same iron, when fashioned into a vessel, causes others to cross and crosses by itself.
Thus it was said regarding the purification of the mind in the *Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa*, verse 40.59.
The discerning extract water by means of water itself, a thorn by means of a thorn, and likewise passion by means of passion alone. (60)

Just as a mirror, when thoroughly cleansed and rubbed free of dust, becomes perfectly pure, so too, when cultivated by the wise, does this [treatise] become the destroyer of suffering within suffering. (61)
The Exposition on the Purification of the Mind (Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa) 39:
The teaching of the knowledge of the Omniscient One is for the destruction of all suffering; or rather, it is for one who is free from passion, yet established in the state of great passion. 62.
If [the practice] is not guarded, obstacles arise as well as the loss of accomplishment;
furthermore, various diseases and afflictions arise, and one is reborn in the Raurava hell. 63.
Various kinds of diseases arise indeed from the violation of the samaya.
[In this age], in every house there are heaps upon heaps of books,
and in every monastery there are crowds upon crowds of scholars.
In forest after forest, there are multitudes upon multitudes of ascetics; yet they do not know reality, nor do they possess peace. 64.
Fortunate is that man who, through the realization of the state of the supreme reality, finds no need for the reading of millions of books that merely please the common folk;
he takes as his root the very medicine of eternal life itself.
By means of crushing those who are equal to him, but not by being dull-witted regarding his burden.
Among the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dharma of the Great Sage,
all those who do not know the reality are indeed rendered fruitless.
Loc. cit. *Caturdevīparipṛcchā*, quoted in *Sūtaka*, p. 2; *Yogimanohara*, p. 57; *Amṛtakaṇikoddyota*, p. 120, and elsewhere:
"He whose intellect proceeds toward the knowledge of the elixir of mercury (*rasarasāyana*), him alone I call a man; what is the use of others? (67)
Listen, O Keśava, the study of the Vedas and Śāstras is not for the sake of knowledge;
once one has become mastered by the knowledge of Brahman, what is the purpose of recitation?
It is stated in the Hariharasaṃvāda: || 68 ||

What is the use of the Vedas, the Smṛtis, the recitations of the Purāṇas, or the highly extensive poems that yield as their fruit only residence in a hut within the village of heaven, or the bewildering performance of ritual acts—
unless one abandons all these for that single fire of destruction at the end of time which utterly consumes the painful construction of the burden of worldly existence?
The merchant continues his business with the remaining goods, while calculating the entry into the state of ignorance regarding his own self.
This has been stated in the Saiva scriptures: [verse 71 or 74].
Wherever one should fix the mind and meditate upon the supreme state, there alone is perfection attained; what is the fruit of a king’s net?
Śucikaraṇa 81; also Yogāmbaramahātantra 119: The great jewel, the wish-fulfilling gem, bestows the fruit of desired objects;
that very same mind, when purified, bestows the fruit of the awakening of a Buddha.
It is said in the *Hevajrapañjara*: [71]
The flow of flavors has been cut off, the senses have been given over; the body has been made into a thorn by Time.
Day and night there is anxiety, delusion, and hatred.
One who is not protected by the Yamunā attains suffering. || 72 ||
O each and every young woman, do not conceive; the life of worldly people is a false essence. One lives for but a moment in this cycle of existence.
Consider the core of the plantain tree; it has no essence. || 73 ||
Do not undertake the practice of going to the source of the Gaṅgā, nor the observance of vows, nor the giving of gifts;
listen to everything according to the view that stands outside of [mere] knowledge.
Liberation does not occur even after a hundred births. || 74 ||
Also quoted in *Amṛtakaṇikoddyota*, p. 174:
"Begone, O King of Delusion!
The Lord of Sahajānanda prevails."
He who was once intent on crushing the jar of sense-objects now delights in drinking the nectar-essence of wisdom.
This has been stated by Carpaṭipāda: || 75 ||
Through the differentiation of the winds, what here is the body and what is the intellect? Just as the forest-born [creatures] perish, all elements go to their dissolution.
Until the mind has indeed reached a firm resolve. || 76 ||
Withdrawal of the senses, as well as meditation, breath control,
concentration, recollection, and absorption— this is said to be the six-limbed yoga.
Anupamarakṣita, p. 121, [states]: "It is taught in the context of the six-limbed yoga in Guhyasamāja 18.141. || 77 ||

By means of postures (āsana), the yogi destroys physical ailments; by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), he destroys sin; and by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), he always overcomes mental disturbances.
It is stated in the Gorakṣaśataka (verse 54): [The Gorakṣaśataka says:]
Placing the right foot upon the left thigh and the left foot upon the right thigh, binding them firmly with both hands behind the back,
placing the two thumbs at the heart, and gazing at the tip of the nose while keeping the chin level.
Thus, the lotus posture (padmāsana) is said to be supreme for the destruction of disease.
It is stated in the *Adhyātmaśataka*, verse 79, or in the *Gorakṣaśataka*, verses 9 or 12.

Having assumed the cross-legged posture with an open face, the external wind— drawn in and directed toward each other’s teeth— is drawn peacefully into the entire center of the navel within the supreme city;
thus restrained, it removes heat, hunger, thirst, and poison from the excellent body.
A white drop on the forehead, surrounded by vowels, emitting nectar.
It is stated in the *Kālacakra* [Tantra] (4.193): [80]
Various gifts, extensive sacrifices, worship of deities, meditative concentration, moral conduct, complete resort to sacred fords, and the recitation of mantras and the like—
all these do not equal even a fraction of this single practice of breath-recitation (*prāṇajāpa*), which leads to inexhaustible auspicious states.
One should proceed with equanimity toward this [world], solely for the sake of sustaining one's life.
That has been stated in the *Adhyātmaśataka*, verse 81.

Neither meditation, nor mantra recitation, nor ritual implements, nor great maṇḍalas, nor seats, nor fire-offerings, nor the consecration of mantras, nor the invocation of the family of the Victors upon the powder, nor the dispatching [of deities],
grants the accomplishment of mudrās or bliss in the supreme state— except by abandoning attachment to women.
Therefore, that should be meditated upon daily by yogins for the sake of liberation. || 82 ||
Kālacakra 4.227: For a yogin whose mind is thus engaged in the practice of the winds, begging for alms is not appropriate, nor is excessive eating, nor even sleep.
In this samādhi, neither the recitation of mantras nor the forceful suppression of breath, nor study, nor worship, nor even the performance of fire-offerings and other rites should be abandoned.
It is said in the *Adhyātmasāraśataka*, verse 52: [as stated] in the *Adhyātmasataka*, verse 83.
Even in the forest, faults arise for those possessed by passion;
even in the home, the restraint of the five senses is asceticism. One does not engage in action when it is devoid of purpose.
For one whose passion has ceased, the home is a grove of asceticism.
Death is conquered by reality; death is conquered by dharma.
Therefore, contemplation devoted to dharma is the means for accomplishing the stages of awakening.

Without the ritual touching of a sentient being, there is neither loving-kindness, generosity, nor patience; without a true guru, there is no knowledge, and without knowledge, there is nothing that grants liberation. (Samvarodaya 19.26cd–27ab)
Through knowledge one attains liberation; knowledge is obtained through merit.
Merit is for the sake of purifying the mind, and knowledge is the means for self-realization.
The purification of the mind has been explained in [chapter] 98. || 87 ||
Through the practice of the state of selflessness, the meditation on the form of the deity is considered the great worship that propitiates all Buddhas. (88)
A similar verse cited in the *Pradīpoddyotana* as an *ārṣavyākhyāna* (p. 76), and quoted in the *Vasantatilakāṭīkā* (p. 67):
"The unconditioned mind is the phenomenon characterized by enjoyment (*sambhoga*).
That very [mind] is the manifold emanation (*nirmita*), being innate by virtue of its own essential nature."
The five aspects have been explained in the *Pañcākāra*. || 89 ||
The Body-Vajra is Brahmā, and the Speech-Vajra is Maheśvara;
the Mind-Vajra is Viṣṇu, and Vajrasattva is Great Bliss.
It is stated in the *Hevajrapañjikā*: [90]
By "Vajra" emptiness is proclaimed; by "Sattva," compassion is remembered.
Through this union of wisdom and skillful means, he is called Vajrasattva. (91)
Firm, substantial, not porous, characterized by being uncuttable and indivisible, neither burnable nor destructible—emptiness is called the diamond (vajra). 92.
Having come and having gone, he remains pervading the universe;
because of the cessation of coming and going, he is known as the Tathāgata. || 93 ||
The glorious one has gone into suchness and likewise returned from it;
by virtue of this wisdom and logic, he is called the Tathāgata. 94.
The yoga consisting of wisdom and means is you; it is the imperishable avadhūtī.
O Yogāmbara, the lunar dust is to be accomplished by that very self. 95.
The vow is the supreme bliss, the unattainable and invisible awakening;
it is the secret of all Buddhas, the assembly, and the vow itself. 96.
The word "vā" signifies that which transcends the path of speech, devoid of the forms of the letters *rā* and *kā*, the emptiness struck by the syllable *hī*; she is celebrated by the name Vārāhī.
The syllable *he* is known as compassion, and emptiness is called the *vajra*;
the non-duality of these two is declared to be *Hevajra*. (98)
Emptiness is expressed by the syllable *a*, great bliss by the syllable *ca*, and the unity of these two by the syllable *la*; therefore, homage be to you, O Acala! (99)

Having bowed to the Guru, Lokeśvara, the protector of all worlds, who is the non-dual supreme embodiment in which emptiness and compassion are inseparable; [I praise] the *Acalakramadvayastotra*. (100)
A being established in awakening is called a bodhisattva;
one filled with the essence of great bliss is designated a mahāsattva. 101.
*Ṣaṭsāhasrikāhevajraṭīkā* 3.3abcd: For the single true self (bhūtātman) indeed appears as five hundred forms;
it is seen both as one and as many, like the moon in water. (102)
Dharma is destroyed by hypocrisy; austerity is destroyed by anger;
knowledge is destroyed by lack of steadfastness; and sacred learning is destroyed by negligence. 103.
For those whose minds are virtuous in every respect, prosperity is found at every step; for those whose minds are defiled by impurity, even their dreams lack prosperity.
It is stated in the *Bharathalīśataka*: || 104 ||
Just as fire situated within the heart of wood does not emerge without friction, so too enlightenment is not born in this life without spiritual practice. 105.
Likewise, within the body, the immutable bliss is situated in various locations;
it pierces the mind, which is tormented by the fire of desire, from all sides.
Because of the mental agitation caused by millions of mantras, there is indeed but one innate mantra (sahaja-mantra), wherein speech, intellect, and mind are dissolved. 106.
Having purified past karmas, both those produced by afflictions and those not produced by afflictions,
this bliss arises like the sun in the darkness.
It is stated in the *Amṛtasiddhi* (22.3) regarding the *amṛtasiddhi-yoga*: [107]
What is the use of deities as objects of focus for those who possess the yoga that relies upon the true nature of reality?
Through the commitment (samaya) of the yoga of the self, the supreme unchanging (paramākṣara) is accomplished. || 108 ||
In the *Vajrasattvasādhana*, following the modified *Śamvara* 1.20:
"As long as the wind, having pierced the knot, does not enter the central channel (*madhyamā*),
for that long the mind remains stainless through the manifestation of the spoken mantra."

As long as one does not take refuge in the supreme vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) by attaining stability in the *bindu*, so long—no matter how much [one may speak]—it is all nothing but truthless, deceitful, and false prattle. 109.
The maṇḍala is said to be the essence, the bodhicitta of great bliss;
because it performs that taking up, the maṇḍala is considered to be a gathering. (110)
Hevajra II.iii.27: Karpūra is indeed Nairātmyā; bliss has the form of Nairātmyā.
Her bliss, Mahāmudrā, is established in the circle of the navel. 111.
Form, sound, as well as smell, taste, and likewise touch,
and that which has the nature of the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu), are enjoyed by means of wisdom alone.
In the *Hevajrapañjara*, *Hevajra* II.iv.44, [it says]: 112.
She alone is the innate form, the Great Bliss, the divine Yoginī;
she alone is the mandala-circle, whose nature is the five wisdoms.
That has been stated in the *Hevajra*: 113.
If the merit of the vow of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is considered to have form, it would fill the entire realm of space and stand even further beyond it. || 114 ||
Also quoted in Tātparyavyākhyā (Tatakaragupta) 13r: The thorough knowledge of all phenomena is not cultivation at all;
the great awakening of great bliss is likewise the supreme Mahāmudrā. (115)
Those who abide in the state of a monk, those men who are devoted to logic, and those who abide in old age— for these one should not teach the reality. (Samvarodaya 3.15cd–16ab)
The locus of this citation is unknown; it is frequently quoted as scripture in the *Sūtaka* and the *Tattvasiddhi*:
"Just as a form endowed with all its limbs appears most clearly in a mirror or a reflection..."
The body of Vajradhara is likewise always enriched with the eighty secondary marks and the [thirty-two] major marks. (117)
